description: Toy Box Friends G5-04: a tour of the respiratory and circulatory systems on a see-through toy body: the air path, the great swap in the air sacs, the heart pump and the figure-8 loop, and an exercise test. No blood or gore: blood is dots.

meta.title: Body Systems Tour: heart and lungs

youtube.title: How Your Heart and Lungs Work Together | Body Systems for Kids | Grade 5 Science | Toy Box Friends
youtube.description:
Thump-thump! Monkey thinks his lungs pump his blood. Robo takes him on a tour of a see-through toy body to find out what really happens.
You'll learn: body systems are teams of organs; the air path (nose, windpipe, bronchi, lungs, air sacs) and the diaphragm; the great swap (oxygen in, carbon dioxide out); the heart's two sides and one-way valves; arteries, veins and capillaries; and why your heart beats faster when you exercise. Blood is shown as colored dots: real blood is always red.
Try at home: find your pulse with two fingers on your wrist, count for 15 seconds and multiply by 4. Press gently, exercise only if you feel well, and stop and tell a grown-up if you feel dizzy.

do.text: Body Systems Tour: heart and lungs
Listen. Thump-thump, thump-thump. What do you think is making that sound?
Phew! That's me after the race! Thump-thump, thump-thump!
My lungs are pumping my blood so fast!
Your lungs? Hmm. Which part really pumps the blood? Let's take a tour and find out.
Your body has systems. A system is a team of organs that work together.
body system
The skeletal system: bones hold you up.
The muscular system: muscles move you.
The digestive system gets energy from food. The nervous system sends messages from your brain.
Today we visit two systems.
The respiratory system, for breathing...
...and the circulatory system: the heart, blood vessels and blood.
I have a battery, not a heart. But living bodies need oxygen every second.
The systems need each other.
Your muscles can't move without oxygen from the lungs, carried by the blood.
Follow a yellow air dot. Air comes in through your nose or mouth.
It goes down the windpipe, also called the trachea.
The windpipe splits into two bronchi, one for each lung.
Inside the lungs, the tubes get smaller and smaller, like an upside-down tree.
They end in millions of tiny air sacs.
Under the lungs is a sheet of muscle: the diaphragm.
When you breathe in, does the diaphragm move up or down? Have a guess.
Breathe in: the diaphragm tightens and moves down. The chest gets more room, and air flows in.
Breathe out: it relaxes and moves up, and air flows out.
Hand on my belly. In... my belly moves out. Out... it goes back!
Fun fact: your left lung is a little smaller, to make room for your heart.
Let's zoom in on one bunch of air sacs. They look like a bunch of grapes.
Tiny blood tubes called capillaries wrap around them.
capillaries
Yellow oxygen passes from the air sac into the blood. The blue dots turn red!
Grey carbon dioxide passes from the blood into the air sac, and we breathe it out.
That's the great swap: oxygen in, carbon dioxide out.
O₂ in, CO₂ out
Fun fact: your lungs have hundreds of millions of air sacs.
Now, Monkey's claims. Do the lungs pump the blood?
No. The lungs swap gases. Another organ does the pumping.
And we breathe out only carbon dioxide, right?
Not quite. Breathed-out air is still mostly the same air...
...just with less oxygen and more carbon dioxide.
Oops! Two mistakes caught. So who does the pumping?
The heart! It's a strong muscle in the middle of your chest, tipped a little to the left.
It's about the size of your fist. Make a fist and look at it!
My heart is as big as this? And it never takes a day off!
Here's a toy cutaway. There are two sides with a wall between them.
The right side pumps blood to the lungs to pick up oxygen.
The left side pumps oxygen-rich blood out to the whole body.
Valves are little one-way doors. They open and close so blood flows only one way.
Lub-dub! That sound is the valves closing.
Arteries carry blood away from the heart. Veins bring it back.
Capillaries are tiny tubes where oxygen and food pass to the body's cells.
So the heart pumps, and the lungs swap!
Fun fact: your heart beats about one hundred thousand times a day.
Now the whole team. Watch the dots go round in a figure eight.
The left side of the heart pumps red, oxygen-rich blood through arteries to the body.
The muscles take the oxygen. The dots turn blue, and the cells make carbon dioxide.
Veins bring the blood back to the right side of the heart, then out to the lungs.
The blue dots are back at the heart. Where do they go next?
To the lungs, to swap!
In the lungs, the blue dots swap and turn red, and go back to the left side again.
Real blood is always red. Our blue dots just mean low on oxygen.
Two loops joined at the heart! Lungs and heart are a team!
I'm Dog, the runner. I'll be the test volunteer!
First, at rest. Monkey, count Dog's pulse for fifteen seconds.
Twenty beats! Twenty times four is eighty beats a minute.
What will happen after one minute of jumping? Higher, lower, or the same?
Let's test it. Jump, Dog!
1 minute, sped up
Thirty beats in fifteen seconds! Times four is one hundred twenty!
And I'm breathing faster and deeper too. Puff, puff!
Working muscles need more oxygen and make more carbon dioxide.
So the heart pumps faster, and we breathe faster and deeper. After a rest, both slow down.
After two minutes of rest, my pulse is almost back to eighty. Phew!
Press gently when you count. Only exercise if you feel well, and stop if you feel dizzy.
Lungs?
Swap the air!
Heart?
Pumps the blood!
Breathe it in, swap it out, lub-dub, pump it all about!
One more time! Breathe it in, swap it out, lub-dub, pump it all about!
How do we keep our team healthy? Move every day. It makes the heart muscle stronger.
Sleep and water help the whole body!
And good food for energy!
Clean air with no smoke keeps the lungs healthy.
What's one thing you can do today to keep your team healthy?
I'll play outside and drink water. And no more racing without a rest!
Question one. Which organ pumps blood round the body?
The heart!
Question two. What happens in the tiny air sacs?
Oxygen goes into the blood, and carbon dioxide comes out.
Question three. Where does the right side of the heart send blood?
To the lungs, to pick up oxygen.
Question four. Which muscle moves down when you breathe in?
The diaphragm.
Question five. Why does your heart beat faster when you run?
Your muscles need more oxygen, so the blood must move faster.
Recap! Lungs swap the air. The heart pumps the blood.
Arteries go away, veins come back. They work as a team, and exercise speeds them up.
